title: Raines v. Byrd (1997)
summary: Individual members of Congress lack standing to challenge a statute on the ground that it dilutes their institutional voting power, even when Congress purports to authorize the suit.
notes:
Key line: "[T]here is a vast difference between the level of vote nullification at issue in Coleman and the abstract dilution of institutional legislative power that is alleged here." Chief Justice Rehnquist, for the Court.

Citation: 521 U.S. 811 (1997).

sections.Parties: Appellants were Franklin D. Raines, Director of the Office of Management and Budget, and Robert Rubin, Secretary of the Treasury, the executive officials responsible for implementing the Line Item Veto Act. Appellees were six members of the 104th Congress who had voted against the Act: Senators Robert Byrd, Carl Levin, Daniel Patrick Moynihan and Mark Hatfield, and Representatives David Skaggs and Henry Waxman. Both Houses of Congress filed briefs opposing the members' suit. The members claimed that the Act injured them by diminishing the effectiveness of their votes on appropriations bills and by altering the constitutional balance between the branches.
sections.Material Facts: The Line Item Veto Act, enacted in April 1996 and effective January 1, 1997, authorized the President to cancel certain items of discretionary spending, new direct spending and limited tax benefits after signing a bill into law, subject to a disapproval bill that Congress could pass by majority vote and that the President could veto. Section 692 of the Act provided that any member of Congress or any individual adversely affected could bring an action in the District Court for the District of Columbia and take a direct appeal to the Supreme Court. The six members filed suit the day after the Act took effect. At that time the President had not yet exercised the cancellation authority.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the District of Columbia denied the Government's motion to dismiss, holding that the members had standing because the Act diluted their Article I voting power and that the claim was ripe. On April 10, 1997, it granted summary judgment to the members, holding the Act unconstitutional under the Presentment Clause and as an unlawful delegation. The Government took a direct appeal under the Act's expedited review provision. The Supreme Court heard argument on May 27, 1997, and on June 26, 1997 vacated the judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
sections.Issue: The Line Item Veto Act expressly authorized any member of Congress to sue over its constitutionality, and six members who voted against it sued the day after it took effect, before the President had cancelled any spending item. They claimed the Act made their votes on appropriations bills less effective and altered the balance of power between the branches. Do individual members of Congress who voted against the Act have Article III standing to challenge its constitutionality on the theory that it diminishes the effectiveness of their votes and their institutional power, notwithstanding the statutory grant of a right to sue?
sections.Holding: No. The members alleged no personal, particularized injury. Their claimed harm was an abstract dilution of institutional legislative power shared equally by all members, not a loss of something to which they were personally entitled. Coleman v. Miller, which upheld standing for legislators whose votes had been completely nullified, does not reach a claim that future votes will be less effective. Congress's grant of a right to sue could not supply an injury that Article III requires. The judgment was vacated.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist stressed that standing must be met with special rigor when a court is asked to hold an act of Congress unconstitutional at the behest of another branch. Standing requires an injury that is personal, particularized and concrete. Powell v. McCormack allowed a member excluded from his seat to sue because he lost something personal: his seat and salary. The appellees here had not been singled out; they claimed an institutional injury that damages all members equally and is based on a loss of political power. Coleman v. Miller was the only precedent upholding legislator standing for institutional injury, and there the legislators' votes had been enough to defeat ratification of a constitutional amendment and were treated as nullified. The appellees' votes on the Act itself were counted; they simply lost. Their claim that future appropriations votes would mean less was a vast step beyond Coleman. History confirmed the result: in past clashes over the Tenure of Office Act, the legislative veto and the pocket veto, no official sued on a claim of diminished official power. The Court noted that the members had not been authorized to represent their Houses, which opposed the suit, that Congress could repeal the Act, and that a person who suffered a concrete injury from a cancellation could bring a proper challenge.

topics.lrs-n-standing-congress: Express authorization cannot dispense with a constitutionally qualifying injury.
topics.lrs-n-standing-constitutional: An institutional loss does not automatically become a personal injury of each legislator.
topics.lrs-n-standing-generalized: The Court treated the legislators' institutional-vote-dilution claim as an abstract, undifferentiated injury shared by every member of Congress.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 7 to 2. Justice Souter concurred in the judgment, joined by Justice Ginsburg, reasoning that the dispute was an intragovernmental one that courts should avoid when other plaintiffs with concrete injuries would soon be available. Justice Stevens dissented, arguing that the Act deprived each member of the constitutional right to vote on bills that become law in their entirety, an injury Coleman recognized. Justice Breyer dissented, arguing that the members' injury was concrete enough and that the case fell within Coleman.
